_comment: Pieces wanted by name, whatever the ranking says (replan §2.2, docs/02 Part D8).
Two groups. The seven rock-module songs are the reason the rock track exists at all — the
owner named them — and each currently has an import placeholder in the catalog with no
file behind it. The Beautiful suggestions are the pieces the Stage-6 'beautiful piece'
project is written around.
Every one of them is in copyright as a composition. That is exactly why they are here and
not in the quotas: docs/00 D23 says the personal build may carry what the dataset marks
public domain, and --strict-license refuses them, so a kept one replaces the placeholder
in the owner's build and leaves the placeholder standing in the public one.
`id` is the catalog id a kept file takes over — the seven rock ids are the placeholders
that are in the catalog today, checked against it by a test, because a want that names an
id nothing has would quietly create a second row instead of replacing the first. The
`song.beautiful.*` ids have no placeholder yet and are new. `title` and `artist` are folded substring
patterns — PDMX titles carry the arranger, the difficulty and the word 'piano' about half
the time, so an exact match would find nothing.
`verify` is a second list and a different job. These are the 34 Part F tunes P5 skipped
for want of an edition to check a melody against (docs/decisions/2026-09-05-p5-authored-
content.md §1). They are not wanted as repertoire — most are four bars of melody — they
are wanted as the *reference* an authored ABC is checked against, which is the
verification P5 lacked and the biggest single gain at this owner's level.
Measured on the first real run: 28 of the 34 have at least one candidate in the archive,
and 25 of those were below the quota line, which is why they need a list of their own.
Admitted outside the quotas, like the wants.
A third group, added 2026-09-12: four jazz standards the jazz ladder is written around.
jazz.5 names them as repertoire and jazz.6 says outright 'nothing in the catalog yet ...
import a lead sheet of one', which leaves four rungs of a repertoire track with no music
on them. Unlike the two groups above these are genuinely public domain in the US - Some
of These Days 1910, Ja-Da and After You've Gone 1918, Avalon 1920 - so a kept file
survives --strict-license and reaches the public build too.
No placeholder rows were added for them. A catalog row with no file behind it is what the
seven rock rungs were, and they were struck for it: a rung whose music never arrives is
not a rung. These are wants until a file exists, and the lessons already say so honestly.
Third group, 2026-09-13: the public-domain repertoire for the blues, jazz and latin
rungs, which between them offered almost nothing to play. blues.6 to blues.9 had no
songs at all — four rungs, levels 5.4 to 8.4, teaching boogie and the twelve-bar form
with no twelve-bar to play — and the latin rung's repertoire was a blues shuffle,
Greensleeves and Row Row Row Your Boat.
Each was looked up as the standard repertoire for what its rung teaches and then found
in the archive index before being written here, with the level the index gives it, so
the rung named beside it is a band the piece actually fits. Nothing in this group is a
guess that something might be in the dataset.
All of them were published in 1930 or earlier and are therefore public domain in the US
under the 95-year term, so they can ship in the strict build as well as the personal
one — which is the point: the tracks that had no repertoire are the ones where the
public-domain material is richest.
Two rungs got nothing and should stay as they are. jazz.6 (6.1-6.4, comping and walking
bass) and blues.8 (6.2-8.3, the form in twelve keys) have nothing suitable in the
archive: what sits in those bands is anime and game arrangements with 'blues' or 'jazz'
in the title, modern transcriptions still in copyright, and uploader improvisations. An
empty rung that says so is better than a rung filled with the wrong music, and both
lessons already say so.
The three sonatinas are a third group and a different reason again. classical.5 is built
on sonata form — its finder asks for it, its 'how you'll know' asks for one movement to
tempo — and not one of the twelve pieces on that rung is a sonatina, or in sonata form at
all; classical.6 and .7 carry the form forward with the same gap. The learner cannot do
what the rung asks with what the rung has.
These are public domain and would never win a quota: the classical bucket is the most
crowded one in the archive and a teaching sonatina loses every ranking to a Chopin
nocturne. That is the whole point of this list. Each `title` pattern was checked against
the 37,499-row index and matches exactly one row, so none of them is a guess:
Clementi op. 36 no. 1   level 4.9  38 bars, two staves, 4.83 from 3 ratings  -> classical.5
Beethoven WoO Anh. 5 F  level 5.5  71 bars, 4.78 from 25 ratings             -> classical.6
Diabelli op. 168 no. 1  level 6.6  53 bars, 4.85 from 71 ratings             -> classical.6/.7
Until a quarry run brings them in, the lessons say plainly that a sonatina has to be
imported and name these three, rather than claiming pieces the library does not have.
